newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russians,Chechens urge restraint despite violence.
newsitem.headline: Russians,Chechens urge restraint despite violence.

text.p: Russian and Chechen separatist officials called on Wednesday for top-level peace talks to seek a stable political relationship after a spate of violence including fatal bomb attacks and the murder of an official.

An emergency meeting in the war-shattered Chechen capital, Grozny, between Russian Security Council secretary Ivan Rybkin and Chechen First Deputy Prime Minister Movladi Udugov produced a joint call for President Boris Yeltsin and Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov to meet as soon as possible.

"Both sides categorically condemn the terrorist acts in Armavir and Pyatigorsk and consider that there could be no justification for the organisers and executors of those barbaric acts," said the joint statement.

A week ago a powerful bomb killed two people in the southern Russian town of Armavir. Another two people were killed and 20 were wounded on Monday when a bomb badly damaged the railway station in the spa resort of Pyatigorsk, also near Chechnya.
Russian Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov said on Tuesday police had detained two Chechen women suspected of organising the Pyatigorsk blast. Grozny has flatly denied any involvement.
The Russian-Chechen statement said a joint commission should be set up to investigate the blasts and vowed to press on with the search for a lasting peace deal.
"The sides appeal to the presidents of Russia and Chechnya to protect the peace process and meet soon to resolve major questions of the political settlement," the document said.
Russia and Chechnya agreed a ceasefire last summer after 21 months of war in which tens of thousands were killed, but talks on a political and economic settlement have since stalled.
Maskhadov wants full independence. Moscow will not grant that and is holding back funds to rebuild the Chechen economy until a final peace accord is signed.
The situation around Chechnya has deteriorated badly in the past week.

Apart from the two bomb incidents, unidentified gunmen shot dead Khamzat Dzeitov, deputy interior minister of the ethnic republic of Ingushetia, bordering Chechnya, on Wednesday. His driver was also killed.
Interfax news agency quoted Russian security sources as saying police had also found and disarmed two car bombs in Ingushetia's capital, Nazran.
On Tuesday, Russian police fought a brief pre-dawn skirmish with a group of what they said were 20 Chechen fighters just outside Chechnya, resulting in casualties on both sides.
But both sides appear eager to continue talks.
Kulikov said after meeting Yeltsin at the Black Sea resort of Sochi that police were taking steps to reinforce security in southern Russia but were not planning to send any fresh troops.
Two of Yeltsin's senior security aides, Rybkin and Boris Berezovsky, rushed to Grozny to meet separatist leaders in a clear attempt to keep up the political dialogue.
Tass quoted Rybkin as saying before starting the talks that there were forces aiming to keep up hostility.
"Many people in Chechnya and in Russia want to disrupt the fragile peace, but we shall block such attempts," Rybkin said without specifying whom exactly he meant.

Kulikov, who appears to be sticking to a tougher line on Chechnya than other Russian officials, said that the Grozny authorities could not control the situation in their own region and had rejected Moscow's help.
"We have taken certain measures to prevent the infiltration of criminals from Chechnya," Kulikov said. "But this does not mean at all sealing off the border between Russia and Chechnya."
"What we want is a full control over it," he added.
